research_rationale:
Identity. The held Federal Register text (14 FR 289, issue of January 20, 1949, PDF page 1) is headed Executive Order 10029. It creates an emergency board under section 10 of the Railway Labor Act to investigate the dispute between Northwest Airlines, Inc. and certain of its employees represented by the International Association of Machinists, and it is signed by Harry S. Truman at The White House, January 19, 1949. The Civil Service Commission notices printed below the order on the same page are separate documents and are not part of the order. Inventory. The order is one block of text with four commands: create a three-member board, bar members from any interest in an employee organization or carrier, require the board to report within thirty days of the order, and forbid any change except by agreement in the conditions out of which the dispute arose from the order's date until thirty days after the board has made its report. I read the whole text; the verified one-clause inventory covers all of it and no operative sentence lies outside it. End. The last command to end is the no-change command, which by its own terms runs until thirty days after the board made its report. The report date comes from the dated letter of transmittal of Presidential Emergency Board report No. 67, held as PDF bytes (jobs/astra-source-retention/output/pdf/afc5c581e901d6a22180aebbd1dcba9cf853d1b4301b339fc05a647b158bbee9.pdf, SHA-256 verified) and cited here as a reviewed factual event. The letter is dated Casper, Wyoming, March 10, 1949 and says the board submits its report herewith; I read the page image, which shows March 10, 1949 (the text layer misreads the month). Thirty days after March 10, 1949 is April 9, 1949 (21 days remain in March after the 10th, and 9 more fall in April). I record the end as April 9, 1949, inclusive of that day, under the owner ruling of 2026-10-21; the exclusive reading, under which the command ends when April 9 begins, is the alternative. The letter date is the date of submission; receipt by the President may have been later, and no held source gives a receipt date. Recited events. The same letter recites that the President extended the board's time to report by thirty days by an order dated February 11, 1949. That order is not held, and it affects only when the report was due, not the thirty-day measure, which runs from the actual report; it is not claimed as an event. Later pages of the held report record that the parties settled the dispute by an agreement placed in the record, and that the chairman received the joint certificate of ratification on March 10, 1949. The no-change sentence permits changes by agreement, so the settlement is not a source that ended the sentence earlier; I found no held source showing an earlier end. Later events. Executive Order 12553 (signed February 25, 1986, 51 FR 7237, Federal Register of March 3, 1986) lists this order by number in a table of orders revoked together with any amendments to them; it came 37 years after the own-terms end and is recorded as the formal disposition. No amendment of this order is held. Searches. The U.S. Code search (release point through 2026-10-09), the eCFR search as of 2026-10-14 and the Office of the Federal Register disposition-note search returned no other instrument affecting this order. Savings: none found.

Identity. The held Federal Register text of Executive Order 10138, signed by Harry S. Truman at The White House, July 3, 1950, creates an emergency board under section 10 of the Railway Labor Act to investigate the dispute between the Toledo, Lorain & Fairport Dock Company, a carrier, and certain of its employees represented by the International Longshoremen's Association, A. F. of L.. Text printed on the same Federal Register pages outside the order is not part of it. Inventory. The order is one block of text with four commands: create a three-member board, bar members from any interest in an employee organization or carrier, require the board to report within thirty days of the order, and forbid any change except by agreement in the conditions out of which the dispute arose from the order's date until thirty days after the board has made its report. I read the whole text; the one-clause inventory covers all of it and no operative sentence lies outside it. End. The last command to end is the no-change command, which by its own terms runs until thirty days after the board made its report. The report date comes from the held NMB report PDF jobs/ptolemy-custody/output/raw/7e200439f16974842877b4a7398f8fec1a110094122d00e66e516fab12c6080d.pdf (SHA-256 verified), Presidential Emergency Board report Nos. 87 and 88 (joint report) (NMB case A-3380-3430), through a source excerpt of its cover page and transmittal letter. The letter is dated August 11, 1950 and says the board submits its report herewith. I also read the page image of the letter, which shows the date cleanly; the text layer of the excerpt garbles the year or lacks the line, and the cover page in the same excerpt carries the date. Thirty days after August 11, 1950 is September 10, 1950 (20 days remain in August after the 11th, and 10 more fall in September). I record the end as 1950-09-10, inclusive of that day, under the owner ruling of 2026-10-21; the exclusive reading, under which the command ends when that day begins, is the alternative. Identity. The held Federal Register text of Executive Order 10139, signed by Harry S. Truman at The White House, July 3, 1950, creates an emergency board under section 10 of the Railway Labor Act to investigate the dispute between the Toledo Lakefront Dock Company, a carrier, and certain of its employees represented by the International Longshoremen's Association, Local 158, A. F. of L.. Text printed on the same Federal Register pages outside the order is not part of it. Inventory. The order is one block of text with four commands: create a three-member board, bar members from any interest in an employee organization or carrier, require the board to report within thirty days of the order, and forbid any change except by agreement in the conditions out of which the dispute arose from the order's date until thirty days after the board has made its report. I read the whole text; the one-clause inventory covers all of it and no operative sentence lies outside it. End. The last command to end is the no-change command, which by its own terms runs until thirty days after the board made its report. The report date comes from the held NMB report PDF jobs/ptolemy-custody/output/raw/7e200439f16974842877b4a7398f8fec1a110094122d00e66e516fab12c6080d.pdf (SHA-256 verified), Presidential Emergency Board report Nos. 87 and 88 (joint report) (NMB case A-3380-3430), through a source excerpt of its cover page and transmittal letter. The letter is dated August 11, 1950 and says the board submits its report herewith. I also read the page image of the letter, which shows the date cleanly; the text layer of the excerpt garbles the year or lacks the line, and the cover page in the same excerpt carries the date. Thirty days after August 11, 1950 is September 10, 1950 (20 days remain in August after the 11th, and 10 more fall in September). I record the end as 1950-09-10, inclusive of that day, under the owner ruling of 2026-10-21; the exclusive reading, under which the command ends when that day begins, is the alternative. The letter date is the date of submission; receipt by the President may have been later, and no held source gives a receipt date. The same held PDF is cited for Executive Orders 10138 and 10139; it is one joint report of the board appointed July 3, 1950 for both disputes (cover: boards 87 and 88, NMB case A-3380-3430), with one transmittal letter that names both the Toledo, Lorain and Fairport Dock Co. and the Toledo Lakefront Dock Co. disputes. The bytes are therefore this order's report. The report also records that the board took up further dock disputes at Cleveland and Huron by agreement; those are not disputes of this order. The report says the President extended the date of the report to not later than September 1, 1950; the report was submitted earlier, on August 11, 1950. That extension concerns the due date only. Later events. Executive Order 12553 (signed February 25, 1986, 51 FR 7237, Federal Register of March 3, 1986) lists this order by number in a table of orders revoked together with any amendments to them; it came 36 years after the own-terms end and is recorded as the formal disposition. Searches. The U.S. Code search (release point through 2026-10-09), the eCFR search as of 2026-10-14 and the Office of the Federal Register disposition-note search returned no other instrument affecting this order apart from the events recorded.
